points: This chapter is a kinah, a lamentation - a sad song meant to remind us of the mistakes we made and motivate us to become different people. We usually associate kinos with Yirmiyahu and Eicha, but Yechezkel deliberately frames this chapter as one.

The two images of the kinah, a lioness with her cubs and a vine, are taken straight from the brachos given to Yehuda: the crouching lion and the abundance of wine. The people would recognize them instantly, which makes the twist land harder - something went wrong with these lions and with this vine.

The first cub that rips apart its prey was tearing at the poor - the standing criticism of the final kings of Yehuda, who mistreated the underprivileged. That cub, carried off to Mitzrayim, is Yehoachaz, son of the great Yoshiyahu, who ruled only three months before Egypt took him. The second cub, taken to Bavel, is left deliberately ambiguous - Yehoyakim, or Tzidkiyahu, who at this point had not yet been exiled.

Lions are meant to defend their people; these turned their ferocity inward. The Abarbanel drives this home through the vine: the fire that burns it comes from within. Our destructions have repeatedly come from infighting - the three-way civil war inside Yerushalayim before the Romans even arrived, and enemies who knew and exploited our internal divisions on October 7th.

This kinah was heard in Bavel, at a distance from the events - and distance can be an advantage. Those of us watching tragedy from outside, trying to help however we can, carry an extra responsibility: like the people of Bavel, take the message to heart and become better people for the sake of the Jewish people.
